title: Bacteria don’t outnumber your cells ten to one: it’s closer to even
body: A widely repeated claim says your bacterial cells outnumber your human cells ten to one. A careful 2016 recount estimated about 38 trillion bacteria in a typical adult, against roughly 30 trillion human cells, so the ratio is closer to one to one. Because bacteria are tiny, they add up to only a fraction of a kilogram of your body weight, even though together they carry far more genes than your own genome.

slides.question: By the 2016 recount, how many trillion bacteria does a typical adult carry?
slides.explanation: About 38 trillion, against roughly 30 trillion human cells: around 1.3 bacteria per human cell, not ten.

slides.heading: Where 10:1 came from
slides.text: The ten-to-one figure grew out of a rough estimate from the 1970s, based on assumed bacterial densities in the gut. It was repeated for decades.

slides.heading: The recount
slides.text: In 2016 researchers Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo combined updated measurements of colon contents and cell counts to get about 1.3 bacteria per human cell.

slides.heading: A ratio that moves
slides.text: Most of those bacteria live in the colon, so the balance shifts day to day. Each trip to the toilet may tip it toward human cells for a while.
